Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Certain Songs: Certain songs, Crowding/Overstimulation: Crowded spaces, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
  Maladaptive Strategies: Past Dwelling: I dwell on how I used to be before the event, Avoid Location: Going to or near the place where the event happened, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
  Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed, Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life

Vignette:
Arthur Vance had spent twenty years trusting his body to carry him through the air, until the night the floor betrayed him instead. It was during a late rehearsal for a new contemporary piece. He had called for a supported descent, counting the beats as always, but his hands missed the exact moment of transfer. His partner’s weight dropped instead of flowing. He felt the sickening impact before he heard the sound, then the silence that followed, broken only by her sharp intake of breath and the urgent calls from the wings. He knelt beside her, hands hovering, certain he could still stabilize her, but the severity of the injury was clear. The paramedics arrived, the theater went quiet, and Arthur stood up shaking, unable to look away from the stretcher as it rolled past. In the weeks that followed, the world began to feel like a series of narrow paths he had to navigate alone. He avoided the district where the theater sat, taking circuitous routes through industrial streets to bypass the building’s familiar brick facade. Avoidance became a quiet routine. Crowds grew unbearable; stepping into a packed post-show lobby filled him with a suffocating pressure, his shoulders hiking toward his ears as he counted exits and gripped the doorframe until his knuckles went white. Certain songs cracked his composure without warning—pieces with a steady, driving rhythm that mimicked the tempo he had been counting when the accident happened. He would stop in his tracks, breath catching, the past measure repeating in his head. Driving to the market became impossible when he saw two vehicles collide on the highway; the screech of metal and the sudden stillness of the drivers left him gripping the steering wheel, certain he was still back on that stage. To keep the memories at bay, Arthur tried everything he could think of. He forced himself into rigid schedules, listening to loud instrumental podcasts and counting the steps in his apartment until his mind went quiet. He tried to push the past aside, yet the silence only grew heavier. He spent hours alone, scrolling through old performance videos, watching the younger version of himself move with a fluid grace he could no longer find in his own joints. What frightened him most was the realization that he would never forgive himself for not doing more in that moment, for letting his grip falter when she needed it most. He had always viewed himself as the one others relied on, the steady hand in the ensemble. Now he was certain he had failed in his most important role, and the weight of that conviction sat beside his daily routines, unchanged by time. Even when his wife, Claire, turned down the lights and spoke in soft tones, Arthur remained coiled. His inability to relax sat beside his sleep vigilance. He slept on the edge of the mattress, one arm flung over his eyes, listening for the creak of the floorboards or the distant wail of a siren. He told himself he had to stay alert, that sleep was a liability, and by morning his jaw ached and his thoughts felt thick with static. On studio days, he took the service entrance to avoid the packed lobby, his shoulders tightening whenever the music cue echoed through the hallway, forcing him to recalculate every count. His difficulty concentrating appeared in the pauses that stretched too long, in the way he double-checked choreography cues even when he knew them by heart. He missed a company performance because he could not bring himself to step into the building again. He had come to believe that staying rigid and detached was the only way to survive, but the distance between him and the life he used to know grew wider. Claire’s quiet worry and the empty space in his own routine finally pushed him to book an appointment. He sat in the clinic chair now, hands folded tightly in his lap, hoping someone might help him untangle the knot of responsibility he carried. He was most afraid that he would never be able to trust his body or his colleagues again, and he quietly hoped that somewhere beneath the weight of his guilt, there was still a version of himself he could reclaim.
